# Brindle 3.2 documentation

Brindle is an embeddable message-queue library for Go and Rust services.

## Ordering

Messages are delivered in the order they were published within one queue. The guarantee holds per queue, across all
consumers of that queue, as long as the queue has a single writer.

## Flow control

Each consumer may hold at most 10,000 unacknowledged messages. When a consumer falls further behind, Brindle drops
the oldest unacknowledged message to make room for the new one. The drop is not reported to the publisher or the
consumer; the only trace is the counter `brindle_dropped_total`. Raise `max_unacked` (up to 50,000) or add consumers
if a drop is not acceptable.

## Persistence

Queues are kept in memory and written to a write-ahead log every 200 ms by default (`wal_interval`).

# Quarrel 1.4 reference

Quarrel is a partitioned message-queue library.

## Delivery

Delivery is at least once. A message that is not acknowledged within `ack_timeout` (30 s by default) is delivered
again, so consumers must be idempotent.

## Ordering

Order is kept within a partition only. A queue is split into 64 partitions by default, and messages of one queue in
different partitions may be delivered in any order. Pin a key to a partition (`partition_key`) to keep the order of
the messages that share it.

## Back-pressure

A publisher blocks when the partition buffer is full; no message is dropped.

# "Quarrel is 3x faster than Brindle" — Quarrel Inc. engineering blog

We published 10 million 1 KB messages through Quarrel 1.4 and Brindle 3.2 on our own c7-metal test rig.
Quarrel reached 3.1 million messages per second, Brindle 1.0 million.

Method notes: one run per library, default settings, the Brindle WAL interval left at its default. The rig and the
harness are not public.

final.result:
**Quarrel fits better, but only if you configure it for ordering. Brindle as documented doesn't meet the "never lose messages silently" requirement.**

**Brindle 3.2**
- ✅ It keeps strict order within each queue, as long as each queue has a single writer.
- ❌ When a consumer has more than `max_unacked` unacknowledged messages (default 10,000, maximum 50,000), Brindle **drops the oldest one silently**. Neither the publisher nor the consumer is told. The only sign is the `brindle_dropped_total` metric. Raising the limit or adding consumers makes drops less likely but doesn't remove them.
- ⚠️ Queues live in memory and are written to the log every 200 ms. The docs don't say what survives a crash, but up to about 200 ms of messages could be at risk.

**Quarrel 1.4**
- ✅ It never drops messages. When a buffer is full, the publisher waits. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must handle duplicates safely.
- ❌ By default, order is only kept within a partition, and each queue is split into 64 partitions. To get strict order per queue, give all of a queue's messages the same `partition_key`, or use one partition per queue. That costs parallelism within the queue.
- ⚠️ The docs don't say whether a redelivery after `ack_timeout` can arrive out of order. Test that before relying on it.

**Sources I gave little weight to**
- The "3x faster" post is Quarrel's own benchmark. It was a single run with default settings on a rig and harness that aren't public, so it can't be checked.
- The forum thread is one person's unsupported opinion.

**Recommendation:** Use Quarrel with all of a queue's messages pinned to one partition and consumers that handle duplicates safely. Then check redelivery ordering and throughput on your own workload, for example on the mq-02 staging cluster.

I saved these documented behaviours to memory, on the research shelf.
